title: One Guide and One Inheritance: Father, Son and Spirit
english: … there was no foreign god with them” (Deuteronomy 32:12). And Jeremiah likewise: “And you did not say,” he says, “Where is the Lord who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, who guided you in the wilderness?” (Jeremiah 2:6).

But Isaiah says that it was the Holy Spirit who guided them: “For he led them through the deep,” he says, “like a horse through the desert, and they did not grow weary; and like cattle through a plain, the Spirit came down from the Lord and guided them” (Isaiah 63:13-14).

And Paul teaches that Christ became their guide: “For they drank,” he says, “from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). In harmony with him Jude too writes in his catholic letter: “For the Lord Jesus, having once saved a people out of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe in him” (Jude 1:5).

Here, then, the argument of those who call the venerable Son and the divine Spirit a creature is overthrown twice over: first, because the words that signify the one infinite nature have been spoken in prophecy of each hypostasis; and second, because beside them stands the line “there was no foreign god with them,” that is, none of another substance.

In the same way Moses says: “The Levites shall have no portion or lot in the land; the Lord himself is their portion” (Deuteronomy 18:1-2; Numbers 18:20). And Jeremiah: “He who formed all things,” he says, “is himself the inheritance of Jacob; the Lord is his name” (Jeremiah 10:16). And David in the sixteenth Psalm: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Psalm 16:5).

But Paul, writing to the Ephesians, says that the Holy Spirit is the inheritance: “In whom,” he says, “having believed, we were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance” (Ephesians 1:13-14). Likewise Paul writes to the Corinthians: “Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, and the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but it is the same God who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4-6).

And to show the identity of the Godhead, he not only names the Spirit first here, then the Son, and only then the Father; but he who has just said that God works all things adds a little later: “But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each one individually as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11). So he presents the Spirit clearly and in so many words as God, of one substance with the Father and the Son, and at the same time as free and sovereign in his own right.
We may also hear God the Father, who has said in Isaiah: …

title: Equal Glory, and the Trinity Dwelling in the Faithful
english: … “And I will not give my glory to another” (Isaiah 42:8); while John says, “that all may honour the Son just as they honour the Father” (John 5:23). For he already knew clearly that the glory is not offered up to the Only-begotten and to the Holy Spirit as to beings of another substance.

Again, Mark says, from Christ’s own lips: “For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him the Son of Man will also be ashamed, when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels” (Mark 8:38). Matthew, setting out the same passage, did not say “in the glory of the Father” but “in the glory of the Son,” writing thus: “But when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, when he sits on the throne of his glory” (Matthew 25:31). And in John too he says: “Glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world was” (John 17:5).
That the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit dwell in the faithful because they are of one substance and equal in power; and a reply to the objection of those who think otherwise.

We shall find the oneness of substance of the Trinity, and that all things are possible to it without any difference, in yet another way, if we see that it alone, being beyond even what is immaterial and invisible, can be shared in according to substance, and can fill the temple it has created. And not only does the thing itself belong to it, but the word fits it as well. For being shared in brings with it being unchangeable, and that in turn being uncreated, which is also being without beginning.

But nothing created, as far as the usage of the Scriptures goes, can be shared in by way of participation, or fill a human being in substance; it can do so only in the way that a good or a bad disposition does. For it is by a figure of speech that we say some people are filled with virtue and knowledge, and are able, with understanding, to bring forth the rewards of virtue and knowledge, like those who have received an unmixed share in the grace of the Holy Spirit.

It is attested, then, that the Father, the Son and the Spirit dwell in us; as when Paul, writing to the Corinthians the second time, says from Jeremiah: “For we are the temple of the living God; as God said: I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (2 Corinthians 6:16). And again: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of …” (1 Corinthians 3:16)

title: God Dwells in the Faithful; Satan Only Deceives
english: … God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). And: “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Corinthians 6:19). And to the Ephesians: “That he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner man, so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith” (Ephesians 3:16-17).

And it is as when the Master says in John: “The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you know him, because he remains with you and will be in you” (John 14:17). And again: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).
This will be still plainer to anyone who considers that God the Word, who can do all things, by his own will both remained unchangeable and was carried in the womb by the Virgin.

But they rise up again to object, with a show of reason: “It is written of Ananias, ‘Why has Satan filled your heart?’ (Acts 5:3), and of Judas, that ‘Satan entered into him’ (Luke 22:3; John 13:27).”

To them we must answer that Satan is not shared in, nor does he board the soul, as it were, and ride in it. He fills the one who does not heed the word, “Do not give your foot to be shaken, and he who guards you will not slumber” (Psalm 121:3), by deceiving him, by working evil counsels and a shifty character into him, and by making him a mere by-work of his own wickedness.

In this way he filled Elymas, his son, with the prompting to a satanic deed. For Paul says to him, a man foul in mind and in deeds, brimming with the devil’s villainy and using sophistry against the saints, so that his father, the author of evil, seemed to dwell in him: “O full of all deceit and all villainy, son of the devil!” (Acts 13:10).
So too he filled the false elders, in the matter of the most modest Susanna, with a licentious mind. The text runs: “And the two elders came, full of their lawless intent” (Susanna 1:28).

And so as not to weary the ear with a great crowd of words, we will pass over much that we could say on this point and put it briefly: if this argument of theirs holds, it is time to stop thinking it a great thing that the divine Serenity dwells in the faithful, and to suppose instead that this has its glory in mere appearance.
